title: Episode 318: Charles I: The Divine Right, the Civil War, and the Scaffold at Whitehall
description:
The monumental, tragic life and reign of King Charles I. Endowed with refined artistic taste and profound religious piety, Charles was an unbending absolutist who ruled without Parliament during eleven years of Personal Rule. His imposition of Ship Money and Anglican prayer books on Presbyterian Scotland ignited the Bishops' Wars and the English Civil War. Defeated by Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army at Naseby, Charles refused to compromise his divine royal prerogative. Tried for high treason against his own people, Charles walked out of the Banqueting House at Whitehall on January 30, 1649, wearing two shirts against the winter frost, to meet the executioner's ax with calm Christian majesty. Discover the martyr king.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the only English monarch ever tried and executed by his own parliament: an unbending believer in the divine right of kings whose death transformed a kingdom: King Charles I. Here is George with the tragic story of the royal martyr.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE DELICATE PRINCE: DUNFERMLINE TO WHITEHALL: 1600 TO 1625
Born in November 1600 at Dunfermline Palace in Scotland, Charles Stuart was a sickly, fragile child who could neither walk nor speak until age four, his legs so weak that doctors proposed placing his joints in iron boots. Overshadowed by his dazzling, athletic elder brother Prince Henry, Charles grew up in quiet seclusion, developing an iron willpower through solitary physical therapy and classical scholarship. When Prince Henry died suddenly of typhoid fever in 1612, twelve-year-old Charles was thrust into the role of heir apparent. In 1623, accompanied by his father's handsome favorite, the Duke of Buckingham, Charles traveled incognito to Madrid as 'Jack and Tom Smith' in a romantic, ill-fated quest to woo the Spanish Infanta Maria Anna. Rebuffed by Spanish court arrogance and religious demands, Charles returned to England in anti-Catholic fury. Ascending the throne in March 1625 at age twenty-four, Charles was elegant, dignified, five-foot-four in height, and a passionate patron of the arts who acquired the Gonzaga art collection and commissioned Peter Paul Rubens and Anthony van Dyck to paint divine visions of Stuart majesty. Charles's stutter was a source of lifelong insecurity, causing him to cultivate an icy, formal reticence in public assemblies. His artistic patronage was the most sophisticated of any English monarch: he purchased Raphael's tapestry cartoons, Titian's masterpieces, and Mantegna's Triumphs of Caesar, spending astronomical sums that scandalized puritan burgesses who viewed Renaissance Italian art as popish idolatry. His marriage to Henrietta Maria of France, the fifteen-year-old sister of Louis XIII, alienated English Protestant opinion from the outset, as the Catholic queen brought her own retinue of Capuchin friars and celebrated open Catholic mass at Somerset House.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ELEVEN YEARS' TYRANNY: PERSONAL RULE AND SHIP MONEY: 1629 TO 1640
Charles's profound conviction that monarchs were accountable to God alone collided instantly with an assertive, puritan-leaning House of Commons. In 1628, Parliament forced Charles to sign the Petition of Right, curbing arbitrary taxation and imprisonment. But in March 1629, after MPs physically pinned the Speaker into his chair to pass resolutions denouncing royal popery and illegal tonnage and poundage, Charles dissolved Parliament in fury. For the next eleven years, Charles governed without a parliament, an era remembered as the 'Personal Rule' or the 'Eleven Years' Tyranny'. To finance his government without parliamentary taxes, royal lawyers revived archaic medieval levies, most notably 'Ship Money'—traditionally levied only on coastal towns during wartime—expanding it in 1635 across all inland English counties in peacetime. When Buckinghamshire gentleman John Hampden refused to pay twenty shillings of Ship Money, the landmark test case galvanized national resistance, portraying Charles as an arbitrary tyrant shredding English liberties. The Court of Star Chamber and the Court of High Commission became instruments of terrifying religious and political repression during the Personal Rule. Under Archbishop Laud, puritan critics like William Prynne, John Bastwick, and Henry Burton had their ears brutally cropped in the pillory at Palace Yard, their cheeks branded with the letters 'S.L.' for 'Seditious Libeller', for writing pamphlets criticizing bishops and court masques. When John Hampden was prosecuted in the Court of Exchequer Chamber for refusing to pay Ship Money, seven of the twelve judges ruled in favor of the Crown, yet the narrow margin of victory was viewed by the nation as a moral triumph for parliamentary liberty against arbitrary royal taxation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE PRAYER BOOK RIOT AND THE BISHOPS' WARS: 1637 TO 1640
The fatal spark that brought down Charles's Personal Rule was lit not in England, but in his native Scotland. Under the guidance of his autocratic Archbishop of Canterbury, William Laud, Charles attempted to impose high-church Anglican uniformity across the British Isles. In July 1637, when the dean of St. Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh began reading from the new royal prayer book, a fiery market woman named Jenny Geddes stood up and hurled her wooden stool straight at the dean's head, shouting: 'Deil colic the wame o' thee, out-thou false thief, dost thou say Mass at my lug?' Rioting erupted through Edinburgh. In 1638, Scottish nobles, ministers, and burgesses signed the National Covenant, swearing to defend Presbyterianism with their lives. When Charles dispatched an army to enforce royal authority in the Bishops' Wars, his untrained, ill-equipped English levies were easily routed by veteran Scottish Covenanters. Bankrupt and forced to pay twenty-five thousand pounds a month to the occupying Scottish army, Charles had no choice: in November 1640, he summoned the Long Parliament, unleashing the constitutional whirlwind that would destroy his throne. The Scottish National Covenant of 1638 was signed by thousands on flat tombstones in Greyfriars Kirkyard in Edinburgh, with some Scottish nobles drawing blood from their own arms to sign their names. Charles viewed the Covenanters with absolute, haughty disgust, refusing to make any meaningful concessions to what he termed 'insolent rebels'. When the Short Parliament assembled in April 1640, MPs led by John Pym refused to vote a single penny for the Scottish war until royal grievances were redressed, prompting Charles to dissolve it after barely three weeks, plunging the Crown into financial bankruptcy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ATTEMPT ON THE FIVE MEMBERS AND THE OUTBREAK OF CIVIL WAR: 1642
Led by John Pym, the Long Parliament dismantled the machinery of royal absolutism: it abolished the Star Chamber, executed Charles's chief minister, the Earl of Strafford—a death warrant Charles wept as he signed—and passed the Grand Remonstrance detailing royal abuses. In January 1642, Charles made a catastrophic, unprecedented move: accompanied by five hundred armed soldiers, the King entered the House of Commons in person to arrest five leading parliamentary leaders for high treason. The Five Members had already slipped away by water to the City. Looking across the crowded benches, Charles took the Speaker's chair and asked Speaker William Lenthall where the traitors were. Lenthall fell to his knees in historic defiance: 'May it please your Majesty, I have neither eyes to see nor tongue to speak in this place, but as the House is pleased to direct me.' Charles murmured: 'I see all the birds have flown.' London exploded in rebellion; Charles fled his capital for Hampton Court, and on August 22, 1642, on a stormy hill at Nottingham, Charles raised the Royal Standard, igniting the bloody English Civil War between Cavaliers and Roundheads. The execution of Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, on Tower Hill in May 1641 was witnessed by two hundred thousand Londoners rejoicing at the fall of the royal minister they nicknamed 'Black Tom Tyrant'. Charles had sent Strafford a personal royal letter promising that 'on the word of a king, you shall not suffer in life, honor, or fortune.' Yet when a furious mob of London apprentices surrounded Whitehall Palace threatening the lives of the Queen and his children, Charles broke his word and signed the death warrant, a betrayal of honor that haunted the king's conscience for the rest of his days.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: NASEBY AND THE COLLAPSE OF THE ROYALIST CAUSE: 1645 TO 1646
For three years, Cavaliers under the king's dashing nephew, Prince Rupert of the Rhine, fought Parliament's armies to a bloody stalemate across England. The turning point came in early 1645 with Parliament's creation of the New Model Army: a disciplined, professional fighting force of godly soldiers promoted on merit rather than noble birth, commanded by Sir Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell. On June 14, 1645, the two armies met at the Battle of Naseby in Northamptonshire. While Rupert's cavalry charged off the field to loot the baggage train, Cromwell's 'Ironside' cavalry maintained iron discipline, sweeping the Royalist flank and routing the king's veteran infantry. Charles fled the field, leaving behind his royal baggage train, including his private cabinet of letters revealing that he was negotiating with foreign Catholic powers and Irish rebels to bring troops to England. The publication of The King's Cabinet Opened destroyed Charles's moral standing. In May 1646, surrounded at Oxford, Charles surrendered to the Scottish army at Southwell, who sold him to Parliament for four hundred thousand pounds. The publication of The King's Cabinet Opened by order of Parliament was an explosive propaganda disaster for the Royalist cause. The intercepted private correspondence between Charles and Queen Henrietta Maria proved that the King had actively petitioned the Catholic King of Spain, the Duke of Lorraine, and the Irish Catholic Confederation for foreign mercenary armies to invade England and subjugate his own Protestant subjects. Cromwell's Ironsides at Naseby, singing the sixty-eighth Psalm—'Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered'—swept through the King's lines with unstoppable fury, capturing Charles's entire artillery train and leaving the royalist infantry to be slaughtered or captured en masse.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TRIAL IN WESTMINSTER HALL: JANUARY 1649
Even in captivity at Carisbrooke Castle on the Isle of Wight, Charles remained stubbornly convinced that the realm could not function without an anointed king. He secretly negotiated an 'Engagement' with Scottish factions, sparking the Second Civil War in 1648, which Cromwell crushed in blood at Preston. Furious at what they called 'that man of blood', the Army marched on Parliament in Pride's Purge, expelling all moderate members to create the 'Rump Parliament'. On January 20, 1649, Charles was brought into Westminster Hall to be tried by a High Court of Justice—an act unprecedented in world history. Dressed in black with the glittering Star of the Garter upon his breast, Charles refused to remove his hat or recognize the authority of the court, tapping the floor with his silver-headed cane until the silver head fell off, an ominous moment of silence as no one bent to pick it up. Charles demanded: 'I would know by what power I am called hither... by what authority, I mean lawful?' Led by John Bradshaw, sixty-eight commissioners signed the death warrant, condemning Charles Stuart as a 'tyrant, traitor, murderer, and public enemy to the good people of this nation'. When Charles was brought before Bradshaw's court in Westminster Hall, the King refused to stand or uncover his head, smiling with aristocratic contempt as the clerk read the charges. When Bradshaw addressed Charles as an elected sovereign accountable to his people, Charles retorted: 'England was never an elective kingdom, but a hereditary kingdom for near these thousand years... No learned lawyer will affirm that an impeachment can lie against the King, for all persons in England derive their authority from him.' The legal dilemma was unprecedented: under English common law, the King was the fountain of justice, meaning all indictments ran in his name, forcing Parliament to invent a revolutionary doctrine that the Crown's sovereignty resided in the representatives of the people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SCAFFOLD AT WHITEHALL: JANUARY 30, 1649
On the morning of Tuesday, January 30, 1649, a bitter, bone-chilling frost lay over London. Charles woke at dawn at St. James's Palace, requesting two linen shirts from his loyal gentleman Thomas Herbert, explaining: 'The season is so sharp as probably may make me shake, which some observers might imagine proceeds from fear. I would have no such imputation. I fear not death.' Escorted across St. James's Park by drums and soldiers, Charles was led into the Banqueting House at Whitehall, walking beneath Peter Paul Rubens' magnificent ceiling depicting his father's apotheosis. Stepping out through a shattered window onto a black-draped scaffold erected above the street, Charles found ranks of cavalry keeping the silent crowd far back. Turning to Bishop William Juxon, Charles declared that he died a Christian of the Church of England, stating: 'A subject and a sovereign are clean different things... I go from a corruptible to an incorruptible crown, where no disturbance can be.' Handing his George jewel to Juxon with the single word 'Remember', Charles tucked his long hair into a cap, knelt at the low wooden block, and stretched out his hands as a signal. The executioner severed his neck with a single blow. As the severed head was held aloft, a deep, collective groan echoed across the crowd of thousands. Monarchy in England was abolished; the Commonwealth was born. On the eve of his execution at St. James's Palace, Charles had a heart-rending final meeting with his two youngest children who remained in England: thirteen-year-old Princess Elizabeth and eight-year-old Prince Henry, Duke of Gloucester. Taking the little boy onto his knee, Charles told him: 'Sweetheart, now they will cut off thy father's head; mark, child, what I say: they will cut off my head and perhaps make thee a king; but thou must not be a king so long as thy brothers Charles and James do live.' Little Henry burst into tears, replying: 'I will be torn in pieces first!' Charles gave them his remaining jewels and blessings. His dignified Christian martyrdom on the Whitehall scaffold transformed his memory from an incompetent tyrant into a tragic royal saint, immortalized in the Eikon Basilike.

[Rebecca - Host]
